title: Anderssen – Kieseritzky, London 1851
description: Known as "The Immortal Game," this casual encounter played the day before Anderssen's first tournament round is the archetype of Romantic-era chess: White sacrifices a bishop, both rooks, and finally the queen to mate with just a knight and bishop. Watch how every sacrifice opens a line toward the black king rather than grabbing material — Black's queen and both rooks never even leave the back ranks before it's over.

title: Anderssen – Dufresne, Berlin 1852
description: The "Evergreen Game" is a model Evans Gambit attack: White gives up rook after rook to keep lines open against Black's uncastled king, then offers the queen itself with 19.Rxe7+!? so that a lone bishop pair can force mate. It's a clean illustration that in an open position with the enemy king stuck in the center, tempo and open lines matter far more than the material count on the board.

The famous finish — a queen sacrifice that lets a rook and bishop deliver a smothering-style mate — shows why rapid development beats grabbing pawns.

Watch how Capablanca gives back some material at key moments simply to simplify into a safe, winning position.

It's the canonical example of winning without a single tactical shot.
